This is a 1 to 4 player dice game with a maximum score of 1,000 to 30,000 points. Points are accumulated by rolling: ones, fives, or three of a kind! Three of a kind count only if all three are rolled at the same time.

1 to 4 player dice game.

Maximum Score: 1,000 to 30,000

You may try for a higher score by removing "non-score" dice and rolling them again. This is done by moving the joystick to your left when the arrow is pointing at the die you wish to remove. The arrow itself may be moved by pushing the joystick up or down. After you have removed all the dice you want, squeeze the trigger for reroll.

If you wish to collect score, move arrow down all the way off screen.

I added "Connect the Dots" by Bill Templeton. This Bally BASIC program for the Bally Arcade/Astrocade appeared in the newsletter BASIC Express, The 3, no. 2 (May/June 1981): 18-19. The original intent of it was to improve the coordination and dexterity of Bill's 5-year-old son, Michael.

https://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/300_baud_programs/cursor/cursor.html#ConnecttheDotsBB

Select the number of points needed to draw an outline of any desired object on the TV. Next, select the scale factor. Simultaneously pressing the trigger, while moving the joystick [will place dots] on the screen to form an outline of the desired object, say a horse. This is the part of the game that requires good hand-eye coordination and dexterity, especially for younger children. It is very easy to move the "BLINKING CURSOR" to various positions on the screen; however, it is fairly difficult to place the desired series of dots in the sequence required to outline the object in mind!

Herein lies the real challenge of the game: to learn how to place a series of dots on the screen, some separated by spaces (by moving the joystick without continuously pressing the trigger), to form an interesting, imaginative figure!

Two versions of the program are included in this archive: the initial one and the enhanced version.

Archiving Notes:

- This program was recorded and saved as a digital FLAC file from a 300-Baud cassette tape, but neither me nor Paul Thacker could digitally archive the program.  To be archived, it would have to be typed-in.

txt2prg input.txt output.prg

kcswin -M -L5 -P50 output.prg output.wav

- The initial printing of this type-in program mistakenly credited the author as Gregg Cattanach. This error was corrected in BASIC Express, The 3, no. 3 (July/August 1981): 33.

•    Design & Manufacture PCBs:

o    Source a modern EPROM or EEPROM (compatible with 8K EPROMs from the 1970s).

o    Order a small batch of assembled PCBs or hand-assemble them.

o    Source original or reproduction Astrocade Videocade shells.
o    If unavailable, explore 3D printing or injection molding options.

o    Source or manufacture clamshell or slipcover cases.

A frequency counter, logic probe or oscilloscope would allow you to inspect a bunch of clocks on the motherboard. I could point you to the clocks, to check if they appear as "active".

The diagnostic SetScreen is now in 3 versions (upgrades). The original SetScreen would increase your chances of seeing some kind of colors or graphics on the TV and help you determine if the Microcycler is functioning.

Both of the MCM Design diagnostics Z80 Check and Balcheck (upgraded) require a 7-segment display.

The Z80 Check diagnostic is used to determine if there is an issue with the operation of the Z80 address/data buses.

The Balcheck diagnostic helps determine if there is an issue with the Microcycler, DRAM control lines or a bad DRAM chip.

Both Balcheck (MCM Design upgrade) and SetScreen3 are included in the MCM Design 8KB BalcheckHR programs package, which is documented at BallyAlley.com within the Balcheck section.

The Nutting Manual system description, also at BallyAlley.com, is an excellent overview of the Bally/Astrocade operation.

If the power supplies -5v, +5v, +10v and +12v are okay, you could use an ohmmeter with the motherboard power off, to confirm all 4 power lines and the gnd lines to all chips are intact. This is a very easy/quick check.

If the power supplies, power/gnd lines are ok and the clocks appear active, you're pretty much forced to run more elaborate diagnostic tests.

Note that Allen Schweitzer has access to the diagnostics:
Z80 Check
8KB BalcheckHR package (diagnostics and graphic test demos)
Z80 Halt
Remote ROM

The Bally Service Manual PA-1, which includes the motherboard schematic and components layout, is archived at BallyAlley.com.

> designed?

I designed the PCB to work with modern EEPROMs instead of the original EPROMs, which are becoming more expensive and harder to source. EEPROMs have several advantages over EPROMs:

* Programming is much faster—about one second for an 8K EEPROM versus several minutes for an EPROM.
* They don’t require UV light to erase.
* They have excellent data retention; for example, the chips I'm using are rated for 100 years.

I chose a PLCC-32 package so the chips could be socketed, making reprogramming and upgrades easy. The PLCC format was the only socket that fit inside an Astrocade cartridge. My current setup uses an 8K XICOR X28HC64J, but the PCB pin-out is also compatible with other common EEPROMs like the Microchip AT28C64B. Both can be programmed using an inexpensive USB TL866-II Plus programmer.

I also relaxed the hole dimensions slightly so the boards can be inserted and removed more easily without damaging the plastic tabs on the Astrocade cartridges.

Overall, the new PCB has been working great, and I’m really happy with how it turned out!

22159:
I would have guessed that the Bally logo was removed when the console was "sold" to Astrocade.  Of course, old stock of those and the "fun and brains" tops were likely allowed to be used up.
As someone who's repaired and worked on 100's of controllers, there are differences.  Some of the early models had a thicker black wire.  All of these were copper wire as far as I can tell.  The later models used what I assume to be aluminum wire which is silver in color.
Some of the controller plugs had the Bally logo on them as well, and some did not.  Again, I think the earlier ones tended to have the Bally logo.
Other minor contrasts are wire colors.  On some of them, it's harder to distinguish the red from the orange, and a lot of the red's and oranges don't exactly match up color wise with wires from other controllers.
Also, and again just my assumption here, but whoever put the controller together would solder the red wire to the trigger in a different way and even different locations.
The early models tended to have potentiometers that had a concave bottom, while later models had a flat bottom.  Typically, on the flat bottom models, you cannot get the contacts to separate from the resistor plate to clean it.  So, if your pot function is bad and you have a flat-bottomed pot, you're better off with Deoxit or a fast-drying non-silicone electronic cleaner.  The concave ones will come apart.  I q-tip clean with acetone first, then Everclear, then Goo Gone.  After that I use just the tiniest dabs of white lithium grease and dielectric grease.  Too much and you'll have jitter.
Some pot stems had 2 "C" clips, and some only have 1.  You really only need the one on the top of the mechanism.  I've never figured out why there is sometimes one down by the pot, but I'll put it back on if it's there.
I believe the original pots were 50K.  I also believe that these either became unavailable at some point or became too expensive and that is why most of the time you'll find a resistor soldered onto the contacts where the black and brown wires connect to the pot.  Remove the resistor and the pot will not function normally.  On the very few I have done this to they become hyper-sensitive.  A small movement will make them go all the way in that direction and it's very difficult for game play.
And that's probably more than anyone cared to know about my SWAG's concerning Bally controllers!  :)

In case you missed it, Video Game History Foundation recently launched a
digital library spanning many magazines and artifacts from their collection.
The search can be a bit hit-or-miss as sometimes I will search Bally and it
returns 0 results. But I have found various insights and tidbits throughout.

 

For example, our own Adam Trionto is featured in a blurb from Computer Game
Review (Nov. 1994) in reference to his Orphaned Computers and Game Systems
magazine. I didn't realize Adam went this far back in his love for Bally and
classic obscurities. The author writes, in part: "My favorite piece in the
Orphaned #2 is Adam's discussion of the Bally Arcade/Astrocade system. It
was surely ahead of its time, and who knows what electronic gaming might
have become if a few flaws (and bad timing) hadn't derailed it."  This blurb
led me to research the Orphaned magazine mentioned, and I see Adam has these
all digitized on his Orphaned Games website! Newsletters and homebrew
mailings have always been the most intriguing and insightful to me of all
the content for these various platforms. It also makes me cognitive of just
how many may be lost to time given the scarcity of circulation even 30-40
years ago. On that subject, Adam do you recall how many subscribers you had
to your Orphaned magazine?

 

In Electronic Games #2.4 (July 1983) a reader wrote in about winning a
$2,500 grand prize in a contest sponsored by Astrocade, Inc. and the Seattle
Mariners / White Sox. Nobody who won the cash prizes ever received their
funds as of Feb. 1983 amid the bankruptcy etc.

 

The Bally Users Group (BUG) newsletter is promoted in the June 1983 (Number
11) issue of The Logical Gamer. "Astrocaders unite! That' s right -- now you
can get together with other owners of the venerable Bally system and swap
talk, tips and even software, through BUG. The Bally Users Group. Kevin
O'Neill is President of the Niagara Regional BUG.You'll get more from your

Graphic Modes Pixel Resolution:
low-res 160 x 102
med-res 160 x 204
hi-res 320 x 204

In the med-res mode, the pixels are the same width as low-res pixels, but 1/2 the height of low-res pixels.

The hi-res graphics requires additional circuitry to map the hi-res TV display. The circuitry is centered around four 8 bit shift registers type 74LS166 which takes the hi-res pixel data and feeds the data serially into the Astrocade custom data chip Serial 0 and Serial 1 inputs.

The four 74LS166 chips utilize a 7M (7.159 Mhz) clock at pin 7. To generate the med-res graphic mode, the negated PX (3.555 Mhz) clock is fed into the four 74LS166 C I (chip inhibit) pins 6. This clock is suppose to temporarily inhibit (shut off) the 7M clock at specific times. What happens is the banks 2 and 3 pixel data is prevented from being fed into the Serial 0 and Serial 1 inputs.

Here's the mystery.

As soon as I unplug the red lead, I lose the med-res graphic mode and see the hi-res graphic mode. See PHOTO 1.

I was nearly ready to give up on attempting to implement the med-res option for my 3G LMHi-Res Astrocade. The med-res graphic mode mystery recently posted is no longer relevant.

The other day I checked my Logic Databook's general description for the 74LS166 chip. The description indicated "The clock-inhibit input should be changed to the high level ONLY while the clock input (at pin 7) is high".

The negated PX clock on the Astrocade motherboard is generated at the inverter U6 pin 2 output. A 47 ohm R37 series resistor is also wired to that U6 output. I connected a 47pf and again a 22pf capacitor following the R37 resistor (with one capacitor lead gnded) to see if that connection might create a propagation delay on the negated PX line, enough to generate the med-res graphic mode. Those 2 attempts accomplished nothing.

Yesterday, I used my logic analyzer to examine the "on-times" (low to high transitions) for the 7M and negated PX clocks. Both of these clocks had on–times that looked nearly simultaneous.

I added 2 series logic gates type 7400 (not 74LS00) to the Perkins Engineering's PX inhibit clock scheme to see if delaying the PX on-time some more would generate the med-res graphic mode. See the attached drawing. This new idea works great! I can now use my new temporary hi-res/med-res manual select "test jumper" set up (see attached drawing) to generate the hi-res mode or med-res graphic mode.

I also tried a 74LS08 chip and a 74HCT08 which also will generate a med-res mode. I tried 2 faster 74LS00 chips which did NOT generate the med-res mode.

I will have to do a minor rewire on the two add-in perfboards boards 2 and 3, so the med-res mode can be generated via software by executing an output instruction to port 08H, where:
bit 0 = enables low or hi-res mode
bit 1 = enables med-res mode when bit 0 is set to hi-res.

I tracked the history of the Astrocade.com website from 1998, when it was a place for bands and other performers to play, to now, when it seems to be a legitimate game creation platform named after, to my great surprise-- the Bally Arcade/Astrocade!  I thought that the name of the current Astrocade website was just a coincidence with this game creation platform of the same name.  I wonder why the company went with that name; maybe someone at the company first programmed in Bally BASIC or AstroBASIC?  Wouldn't that be something fun to find out about them?

This post is a little long, but I found it fun to use Internet Archive to reach back through 27 years of the Astrocade.com website.  We'll end up with the current site, which is a platform which can be used to play games.  Here we go!

The archived Astrocade.com website from January 10, 1998 has a plain html "banner" with a description of the Astrocade media website that says:

"The Astrocade is a non-profit collective bringing a myriad of interesting events to the local community. What is an interesting event? So far it has been bands/projects which are not your everyday rock -n- roll, but more along the lines of the experimental, noise, free jazz, psyche, sleeytime ambient, kuckoo, or whatever the cat coughs up. Monetary guarantees are not given; however, we are fair and pay the bands whatever comes in the door."

According to the website, this venue was located at 1021 Ridge Ave. Philadelphia, PA.  You can read more about it here as captured by the Internet Archive:

https://web.archive.org/web/19980110014214/http://astrocade.com/

The site also says that "the following are some of the interests of various members: [Classic Video Games, Motorcycle Repair, and Carpentry.]"  It makes sense that one of the people involved was a classic video game enthusiast.  He must have come up with the name for the venue.

The December 12, 1998 capture from Internet Archive shows that The Astrocade venue is using the Astrocade game console logo for the banner at the top of the page now.  See here:

I honestly don't see the appeal of using "generative AI" to create games.  As I see it, video games (and board games, for that matter) are a work of art more than of logic, and as such are a communication of an idea (or a vision) between game programmer (and artists, composers, etc. for many modern games, of course) and player.  It's really neat to play a fascinating and / or beautiful game and think "Another person made this.  I'm seeing and experiencing what they wanted to communicate!"  If a game is AI-generated, then it's of no more value, as far as I can see, than an oil spill than happens to look interesting for a little bit.  A soulless, cold, simulacrum of art, rather than art itself.


Also, frankly, I can't help but roll my eyes at the buzzword aspects of "AI" in every darn thing everywhere these days, from my washing machine having a little tag that claims that it uses "AI" to clean better (no real explanation given) to products that always used /some/ kind of algorithm to Do A Thing now suddenly being labeled "AI powered!" and such.  It's everywhere, it's flashy, it's marketed as if it were actual magic, and it mostly seems to be some combination of unnecessary and annoying.

For an example:  I bought some roofing materials from Home Depot, and their website wouldn't shut up about how I can ask their AI chatbot questions about products... with a disclaimer stating that I shouldn't trust what the AI chatbot tells me and to be sure to check with the manufacturer of every single product to be sure about its real specs.  My serious question:  If the "AI" isn't programmed to either give a correct answer (presumably taken directly from an official datasheet) or reply with "N/A", then what's the point of even asking the AI anything?  Of what use are LLM "hallucinations" to me when I'm trying to get real specs on real products that I'm going to put into a harsh environment?  So useless!

AI (and that's become SUCH a broad category of related -- and even unrelated -- technologies lately) seems to be proving useful in medical imagine analysis as "a second set of eyes" for disease diagnostics, and a few other things.  But, for most of it, it seems like a processor-time-intensive, electricity-wasting exercise in programmatically generated noise.


Just my two cent, anyway.  :-)


Respectfully,


Derek Christenson
